elements.content: Communication Goal: I can talk about food, ask about quantities, and order a meal.

Lesson overview:
- Level: A0 General English
- Unit: Unit 7. Shopping
- Time: 60 min (Essential) / 90 min (Expanded) / 120 min (Full Workshop)
- Focus: All sorts of diets
- Materials: Food cards, food pyramid, menu, COSYmanuals 'some/any' and 'countable/uncountable' pages.
By the end of this lesson, you can:

• use countable and uncountable nouns
• ask about quantities with how many
• order food politely with would like

Which word belongs to the previous lesson?
Core Active Vocabulary (19 items):

bread — a food made from flour. Example: We have some bread for breakfast.
cheese — a food made from milk. Example: There is some cheese in the fridge.
butter — a yellow food made from milk. Example: I put butter on my bread.
meat — food from an animal. Example: She does not eat meat.
chicken — a bird, or its meat. Example: We have chicken for dinner.
fish — an animal that lives in water. Example: I eat fish on Friday.
fruit — sweet food from a plant. Example: We buy fresh fruit.
vegetable — a plant food such as a carrot. Example: Eat more vegetables.
some — a small amount, used in positive sentences. Example: I have some bread.
any — used in negatives and questions. Example: We haven't got any milk.
how many — a question about countable quantity. Example: How many apples do you want?
order — to ask for food or a product. Example: I order a starter and a main.
menu — a list of food and drinks. Example: Can I see the menu, please?
waiter — a person who serves food. Example: The waiter brings the bill.
bill — the paper that shows what you must pay. Example: Could I have the bill, please?
would like — a polite way to say want. Example: I would like tomato soup.
starter — a small dish before the main meal. Example: I'd like a starter and a main.
main — the largest dish of a meal. Example: The main is chicken and rice.
dessert — sweet food after a meal. Example: We don't want dessert.
Essential Chunks & Functional Collocations:

• I eat fresh fruit and vegetables. (talking about diet)
• I have some cheese and bread. (positive sentence with uncountables)
• I don't eat any meat. (negative sentence with uncountables)
• How many apples do you want? (asking about countable quantity)
• I'd like a starter and a main, please. (ordering food)
• Could I have the bill, please? (asking for the bill)

elements.content: Grammar Focus: Use 'some' in positive sentences and offers, and 'any' in negatives and questions.

Form:
Some vs any: some + plural or uncountable noun (positive/offer). any + plural or uncountable noun (negative/question).

Examples:
• I have some bread.
• We haven't got any milk.
• Have you got any apples?
• Would you like some tea?
Controlled practice: choose the correct form.
I have ___ cheese.
We haven't got ___ eggs.
Have you got ___ fruit?
Would you like ___ coffee?
Substitution drill: say the sentence with the new words.

• I have some ...
• I haven't got any ...
• Have you got any ...?
• Would you like some ...?
Question-answer practice: ask and answer with your partner.

• What food have you got at home?
• What food haven't you got?
• What would you like to drink?
Personalised production: use the structure about your own life.

• Write three sentences with 'some' about your kitchen.
• Write three sentences with 'any' about your bag.
Reading: All sorts of diets

On my diet, I eat fresh fruit and vegetables. I have some cheese and bread, but no meat. My sister doesn't eat any fish. She has some chicken and rice. At the café, I order a starter and a main. I'd like tomato soup and a chicken salad. How many apples do you want? Just two, please. The waiter brings the bill. Could I have the bill, please? Yes, of course.
What does the writer eat?
What does the writer order?
Listening: listen to the dialogue and answer the questions.

A: Good evening. Are you ready to order?
B: Yes, I'd like a starter and a main, please.
A: How many starters?
B: Just one, please. Tomato soup. And a chicken salad for the main.
A: Anything to drink?
B: Water, please. Could I have the bill after that?
A: Of course.
How many starters does the customer want?
What is the main dish?
Speaking task: Interview your partner about their diet. Then role-play ordering a meal.

• What do you eat for breakfast?
• Do you eat meat?
• How many fruits do you eat every day?
• What do you order in a café?
• Do you ask for the bill or pay at the counter?
Role-play: You are at a café. Order a starter, a main, and a drink. Ask how many and ask for the bill.
Work in pairs. Take turns. Use at least five target words and one target grammar structure. Then swap roles.
Writing task: Write a short restaurant order and a shopping list.
Model: I'd like ... How many ...? Could I have the bill, please?
